implementation_notes: business-rules keeps the rule base as plain Python data: fact fields are declared as typed rule variables (@numeric_rule_variable, @string_rule_variable, @select_rule_variable) and effects as rule actions (@rule_action with declared params), then JSON-shaped rules naming a variable, an operator, a value and an action are applied with run_all(rule_list=..., defined_variables=..., defined_actions=..., stop_on_first_trigger=True). Because variables and actions are declared in code, rule data can only use what the developer exposed, and the same declarations can be exported with export_rule_data so a UI can offer exactly those variables and operators. It is the lightest way to let rule data change without a deploy while keeping a typed boundary.
code_sketch:
from business_rules import run_all
from business_rules.variables import BaseVariables, numeric_rule_variable
from business_rules.actions import BaseActions, rule_action
class OrderVars(BaseVariables):                 # declared fields are the rule vocabulary
    @numeric_rule_variable
    def units(self): return self.order["units"]
class OrderActions(BaseActions):
    @rule_action(params={"rate": 0.10})
    def apply_discount(self, rate): self.order["discount"] = rate
rules = [{"conditions": {"all": [{"name": "units", "operator": "greater_than", "value": 100}]},
          "actions": [{"name": "apply_discount", "params": {"rate": 0.10}}]}]
run_all(rule_list=rules, defined_variables=OrderVars(order), defined_actions=OrderActions(order))
pitfalls: Every variable and action a rule names must exist on the declared classes: an unknown name is a runtime lookup failure, so validate rule stores against export_rule_data.
The operator must belong to the variable's type family (numeric or string or select): the library will not reject a string operator on a numeric variable at load time.
Actions receive only their declared params, so anything else a rule needs must come from the object the action holds - which quietly re-couples rules to code.

variants.name: durable_rules forward chaining (Rete)
variants.idiom_name: durable_rules: ruleset + @when_all decorators over a Rete core
variants.implementation_notes: durable_rules is a forward-chaining engine (Rete, implemented in C with Python bindings): rules live inside a ruleset context, conditions are written as Python expressions on the m (fact/event) and s (state) names with @when_all/@when_any, and consequences assert_fact, retract or post further events. Correlated sequences, statecharts and flowcharts let it express policy that depends on several facts arriving over time, which a per-request rule list cannot. The trade-off is a stateful host: facts asserted into a ruleset persist until retracted, so scope the host (or clean up facts) per unit of work.
pitfalls: Ruleset state is per host and long-lived: facts asserted by one request are still visible to the next unless retracted, so hosts must be scoped (or cleaned up) per unit of work.

Pattern matching compiles to a deterministic state machine with no backtracking: only the documented comparison and matches/imatches forms work, and unsupported expressions fail when the ruleset is defined.
The engine core is a C extension: malformed rules or facts surface as core errors, so wrap rule definition and fact assertion in validation and tests.
